paragraphs: Five timer reload words, indexed by the Speed Booster counter times two.
The first word also initializes the adjacent timer/counter pair: its low
byte is the initial delay and its high byte is the starting counter.
Later reloads are ORed into the low timer byte while preserving the counter.
Initial jump velocities for air, water, and lava/acid, in that order.
The integer and fractional components live in parallel speed/subspeed
tables. !SPF scales the velocity for the selected regional frame rate.
Each movement type selects a 12-byte row: acceleration, maximum speed,
then deceleration. Each value occupies two words; wordSwap places the
integer word before the fractional word consumed by the movement code.
SetTimer takes packed BCD minutes and seconds ($MMSS), not binary seconds.
Clear the old countdown before loading the duration and startup state.
SetTimer takes packed BCD minutes and seconds ($MMSS), not binary seconds.
Startup begins with an initial delay before the timer display moves into place.
Fuse countdown loaded for newly fired bombs before their explosion sequence.
regional selects the NTSC or PAL reload value.
Item messages wait for lag frames before accepting input. The collecting
PLM schedules the music-resume delay separately from this message wait.
The regular Zoomer shares its movement state machine with other crawlers.
InitAI_Zoomer_MZoomer chooses its starting orientation; MainAI_Crawlers
dispatches the handler installed by the orientation's animation script.
X is the enemy slot and Y points to the script's next word: a bank $A3
movement-handler address. Consume that word and return Y to the interpreter.
Zoomer/Zeela orientation lists install the handler before their first frame.
Their frame loops skip this command, so they do not overwrite a falling
handler on every animation cycle.
Before initialisation, Enemy.instList holds the population's initialisation
value, not a script pointer. Its low two bits select upside right, left,
down or up (0..3). Replace that value with the matching instruction list,
then fall through to the shared initialiser with X still the enemy slot.
Start with no visible spritemap and a do-nothing handler. An instruction
timer of one lets the orientation script install both on its next update.
Enemy.init0 selects the speed-table word copied into both velocity fields;
$00FF skips the lookup; existing velocities still pass through sign selection.
Crawling velocities are signed 8.8 pixels per frame, unlike the separate
integer/fractional word pair used while falling.
The low two property bits choose the initial velocity signs independently
of the script-orientation value: 0 negates X, 2 negates Y, 1 and 3 leave
both unchanged. These signs are also applied when the speed lookup was skipped.
These four orientation tables use Enemy.init1 directly as a byte offset
(0, 2, 4, 6, 8 or $0A), not an element number. It selects the species' script.
A corner turn chooses a new orientation list and resets the instruction timer
to one; that list installs the corresponding horizontal or vertical handler.
Crawler.function is a bank-local handler address, not a numeric state ID.
Tail-jump with X = EnemyIndex; the selected handler returns with RTL to
the AI caller. Orientation scripts and falling transitions share this field.
On a wall, X velocity presses into the surface and Y velocity moves along it.
A type $0014 earthquake at timer $001E saves this handler and selects falling.
That change does not return early: this invocation still performs its crawl step.
Convert signed 8.8 velocity to the movement helpers' signed 16.16 distance:
clear $12/$14, sign-extend, then store the velocity across $13/$14.
Add one pixel in the X direction to probe wall contact before travelling
along Y. The helpers return carry set on collision; $14.$12 is scratch
for the current move, not a persistent X- or Y-specific variable.
The wall probe collided, but travel along Y hit an inside corner.
Reverse X velocity and choose a floor/ceiling animation from the Y sign.
Restarting that script switches movement to the horizontal handler.
No wall contact: count this unsupported turn. Four consecutive misses
save the current handler and select falling instead of turning again.
Earlier misses reverse Y and select a floor/ceiling script to follow
the outside corner. Finding wall contact resets the shared turn counter.
Falling uses a separate signed 16.16 Y velocity: $14 receives the integer
word and $12 the fractional word. Move first, then accelerate if unobstructed.
A collision restores nonFallingFunction after clearing fall speed and the
turn counter. For the $00FF speed-lookup sentinel, landing first assigns
$0080 (0.5 pixels per frame) to both crawling velocities.
Add $8000 to the fractional word in NTSC, or $A000 in PAL, propagating
carry into the integer word. Acceleration stops once the integer part
is at least four; this test does not clamp an existing overshoot.
On a floor or ceiling, Y velocity presses into the surface and X travels
along it. The same earthquake trigger as vertical crawling saves this
handler and selects falling without skipping the current crawl step.
Expand signed 8.8 Y velocity into $14.$12, then add one pixel in its
direction to probe floor/ceiling contact. With support, calculate the
slope-adjusted X distance and move along the surface. A clear X move
is followed by vertical alignment to a non-square slope.
The support probe collided, but X travel hit an inside corner.
Reverse Y velocity and use the X sign to select a wall-facing script.
Its initial command installs the vertical movement handler.
No floor/ceiling contact: share the vertical handler's unsupported-turn
counter. On the fourth miss save this handler and fall; otherwise reverse
X and select a wall-facing script to follow the outside corner.
Finding support resets the counter before attempting X travel.
Input X is the enemy slot. Sample the supporting edge selected by the sign
of Y velocity. A slope block with BTS subtype >= 5 selects an 8.8 multiplier;
multiply the magnitude of the 8.8 X velocity and restore its sign.
Return the 16.16 move distance in $14.$12 with X restored to EnemyIndex.
Without such a slope, just expand the original velocity to 16.16.
The stored Crawler.XVelocity is not changed by this adjustment.
InitAI_Waver splits the regional horizontal speed and chooses its direction.
MainAI_Waver moves horizontally, derives vertical distance from a wave phase,
and coordinates steady/spinning animation scripts through a completion flag.
Population parameter 1 bit 0 selects left (0) or right (1), not a speed index.
The animation index packs facing in bit 0 and spinning in bit 1.
Indices 0/1 select steady-left/right; 2/3 select spinning-left/right.
newInstListIndex requests a state; instListIndex caches the installed list.
Both spin scripts execute this after their four eight-tick frames.
Signal main AI through spinFinishedFlag; do not change facing or velocity.
There is no parameter word to consume. The following sleep holds the last
spin frame until main AI clears the spin bit and selects a steady list.
The regional 8.8 speed is $0180 (NTSC) or $01D0 (PAL), split into
a signed integer word and a fractional word for 16.16 movement.
Parameter 1 bit 0 set keeps positive X motion; clear negates the full
8.8 value before splitting it. The .facingLeft name marks the common
tail, not the direction of the branch that reaches it.
Seed the steady-left list directly, then request index 0/1 from the same bit.
The animation helper only resets timers when that requested index changes.
Move in X first. On a wall hit, reconstruct the original 8.8 speed from
overlapping velocity bytes, negate it, and toggle facing while clearing spin.
That path skips Y movement and phase advance but still checks animation.
Without an X collision, use the shared negative-sine helper's integer return
as a Y distance; this is phase-driven velocity, not an absolute Y coordinate.
Y collision reflects the phase; otherwise advance it by two before testing spin.
Pass radius 4 and the low-byte phase to the shared negative-sine helper.
Only its signed integer return is used; $12 is zero, so the fractional
sine result is discarded rather than accumulated as vertical subpixels.
A blocked Y move adds $80 and masks to a byte, selecting the opposite
vertical phase instead of taking the normal +2 advance.
Advance the phase only after both X and Y movement report no collision.
The stored word is not masked here: the sine helper uses its low byte,
and the animation test uses its low seven bits. A wall leaves it unchanged.
The low-seven-bit phase test requests spinning at $38 and $B8.
Keep facing in bit 0 and set spin in bit 1. Repeating the same request
does not restart its script because SetWaverInstList compares cached indices.
This check also runs after either collision path, not only after free movement.
Consume the flag set by the spin script after all four frames.
Clear only the spin bit in the requested index, preserving its current
facing, then select the matching steady list. The flag is cleared once.
Switch scripts only when the desired index differs from the installed index.
An unchanged index returns without resetting animation timing, allowing the
spin's frames to finish. On a change, resolve the two-byte table entry,
set instruction timer 1, and clear the previous script's loop counter.
The reset vector enters in emulation mode. Switch to native mode and the
bank-$80 FastROM mirror, establish the stack and direct page, then initialise
low RAM and the display. Upload the SPC engine before joining CommonBootSection.
The polling delay below is retained as written; its original purpose is unknown.
Cold boot and SoftReset converge here. Force blank, clear bank $7E and initialise
CPU/PPU shadows, sound queues and sprite-transfer state before enabling NMI.
Finish the SRAM/demo checks, then jump to MainGameLoop without a return address.
NMI may run before the first frame request; its no-request path skips uploads.
Prepare one game-state iteration, then publish it through WaitForNMI.
Music/HDMA logic and the random seed advance before the state handler; sound
queues and RAM OAM are finalised afterwards. The state-specific handlers choose
which simulation systems run; this loop is also used by menus and cinematics.
The low state byte indexes 45 bank-local word pointers ($00..$2C), with no bounds
check. A state change inside a handler affects the next dispatch, not this call.
Set NMI_Request only after the caller's frame buffers and transfer queues are
ready. NMI clears it after uploads and controller sampling, releasing this
busy-wait. An NMI with no request takes the lag path instead of consuming
partially prepared data. NMI must be enabled or this routine cannot finish.
Processor flags and the data bank are restored; A is used by the polling loop
and byte-index mode truncates the high bytes of X and Y.
Set bit 7 in both $4200 and its shared DP_IRQAutoJoy shadow. Preserve the
h/v-counter interrupt and auto-joypad bits. This is separate from CLI/SEI:
the CPU's IRQ-disable flag does not enable or disable NMI.
Clear bit 7 in both $4200 and DP_IRQAutoJoy, preserving the other control bits.
Keeping the shadow in sync matters because Update_IO_Registers uploads it again.
A subsequent WaitForNMI requires NMI to be re-enabled.
The native NMI vector enters through bank $00; jump to the bank-$80 mirror,
save full-width registers and establish direct page $0000 before doing work.
A nonzero NMI_Request gates the prepared-frame transfers and input sampling.
Servicing it clears the request and lag count and advances NMI_8bitFrameCounter
and NMI_FrameCounter. NMI_Counter advances on both serviced and lag paths.
RTI restores the interrupted processor status as well as its program address.
Refresh the table-address registers for six HDMA-object slots. The object index
steps by two; each active slot supplies a DMA-channel offset and a word pointer.
Later, DP_HDMAEnable is written to $420C after the queued VRAM transfers.
No frame is ready. Leave transfer queues and sampled controller state untouched;
increment the byte-sized consecutive lag count and its unsigned high-water mark.
The count wraps at $100; the high-water mark is retained across that wrap.
Rejoin the common exit to count this NMI and restore the interrupted context
without advancing the serviced-frame counters.
Dispatch h/v-counter IRQ commands for scanline effects such as the HUD split
and door-transition drawing. DP_IRQCmd is already a word-table byte offset.
The command returns its successor in A, the next horizontal target in X and
vertical target in Y. Store all three before restoring the interrupted registers.
Unlike NMI, this entry does not change the direct-page base; direct-page command
state uses the engine's existing direct page.
Schedule the title-sequence loader and choose the initial attract-mode demo set.
The count found during boot normally starts at set 0; a count of four selects
set 3. Increment GameState to 1 and return to the outer frame loop.
Run the normal gameplay handler before advancing the fade-in. Actors and room
logic therefore continue while the screen brightens. When the brightness shadow
is exactly $0F, clear the fade timers and increment GameState (normally 7 to 8).
Order the gameplay subsystems, rather than running every entity from one loop.
Select enemy lists first; Samus's current-state phase precedes interactions and
enemy AI, and her new-state phase follows the main enemy routine. Projectiles,
PLMs, tile animation and collision passes run before scrolling and sprite drawing.
Individual handlers still control their own frozen/disabled behavior. The debug
skip below bypasses this simulation block, but not the shared housekeeping tail.
This tail also runs after the debug skip: HUD and background scroll calculations,
room main ASM, energy/game-time handling, shaking and hurt-timer/list cleanup.
The in-game clock is updated by the called helper, not by counting all NMIs.
Return to MainGameLoop for sound processing, OAM finalisation and publication.
Called near the end of a serviced NMI, after the graphics work. Wait until the
auto-joypad busy bit clears before reading the controller result. Derive newly
pressed buttons from current AND (current XOR previous), then maintain held
button repeat state. The no-request NMI path does not call this routine.
Accept a newly pressed Start only in gameplay state $08, outside Ceres, with
no power-bomb flag, frozen-time flag or enemy-pause door-transition flag set.
Prime the brightness fade and select state $0C; do not load the pause menu here.
Gameplay continues while brightness decreases. Test only the low brightness
nibble for zero, then advance to pause graphics setup. This differs from the
unpause menu fade-out, which waits for the full brightness shadow to equal $80.
Replace the gameplay display while dark: suspend HDMA and animated tiles, back
up graphics state, run the room's pause hook, then load menu tilemaps and colors.
PHP/PHB protect the hook caller; PHK plus PEA form a synthetic long return frame.
The indirect JML uses a 24-bit hook pointer. Its RTL consumes that frame before
PLB/PLP restore the separately saved bank and status.
Draw the pause menu while increasing brightness. An exact $0F shadow means
full brightness with forced blank clear; then clear fade timers and advance
to the interactive paused state. No ordinary gameplay handler is called here.
Maintain timed held/new input, the selected pause page, HUD and palette animation.
This uses MainPauseRoutine, not GameState_8_MainGameplay. The outer main loop
still services music/HDMA logic, sound queues, OAM and the NMI frame handshake.
Dispatch the pause menu's own eight-state machine, independently of GameState.
Indices 0 and 1 are the interactive map and equipment pages; 2..4 switch from
map to equipment, and 5..7 switch back. Double the index for bank-local word
pointers. The table has no bounds check; handlers return with RTS, this entry RTL.
Use the pause menu's timed held/new input stream, unlike PauseCheck's new-only
controller input. Start queues confirmation, primes fade-out and flashes the
button label before incrementing GameState, normally $0F to unpausing state $10.
Refresh the L/R/Start tilemap even when no Start input was accepted.
Keep drawing the selected pause page and pressed-Start highlight while fading
out. Wait for exactly $80 (forced blank set, brightness zero), not just a zero
brightness nibble, before advancing to gameplay graphics restoration.
Rebuild the gameplay display before fading it in: restore saved colors and
graphics state, reload gameplay assets, then run the room's long unpause hook.
PHK/PEA build the hook's RTL return frame; the separate saved bank and status
remain on the stack until after HDMA, animated tiles and movement sounds resume.
Advance GameState before restoring the handler's outer saved processor status.
Run gameplay while the restored display brightens. On an exact $0F brightness
shadow, clear fade timers and explicitly select gameplay state $08.
This state resets to $08 instead of advancing to the next numeric game state.
Reload gameplay graphics while interrupts are controlled for direct VRAM work.
Mask IRQs, stop DMA, disable NMI and h/v-counter interrupts, then rebuild CRE,
tileset, background, visible-room and PLM graphics. Re-enable the interrupt
sources and restore the caller's saved bank and processor status before RTL.
Call the bank-$82 preliminary door/elevator phase using a synthetic near return:
PEA pushes .manualReturn-1 and the indirect JMP reaches a phase ending in RTS.
Carry clear keeps state $09; carry set advances the state and tail-calls
GameState_A_LoadingNextRoom immediately in the same outer-loop iteration.
Ordinary doors and elevators with negative direction finish this preliminary
phase immediately with carry set. The other elevator path selects the regional
downward delay and executes its first timer decrement in the same call.
Decrement the regional delay before testing its sign. A resulting zero still
runs enemies and draws the scene with carry clear; only a negative result
returns carry set to release game state $09. This path draws inanimate Samus
rather than calling her ordinary gameplay state handlers.
Prepare the room transition once before entering the phase dispatcher. Set the
transition flags, choose fade target colors while retaining selected HUD/timer
colors, queue the door sound and inhibit further ordinary sound requests.
Select WaitForSoundsToFinish and advance GameState, normally $0A to $0B.
Later phases return to the main frame loop; the room is not loaded in one call.
Dispatch one saved DoorTransitionFunction per call through an indirect near JMP.
PEA supplies the return word minus one expected by the phase's RTS. Phases may
select another data bank; save and restore the caller's bank around dispatch.
After the phase returns, draw an active countdown timer before the common exit.
Keep running enemies and drawing while all three sound-library queues drain.
Each queue is empty when (next index - consumed index) AND $0F is zero.
This checks queued requests, not whether a sound has finished playing on the SPC.
Only after all three rings are empty select the palette fade-out phase.
Fade palette entries toward the targets prepared by state $0A. This is palette
interpolation, not HandleFadingOut's display-brightness fade. While unfinished,
run enemies and draw the scene; on carry set, schedule door-header/HDMA setup.
Load door metadata, remove old HDMA objects and clear their processing-enable
bit. Request scanline IRQ command $08 through DP_NextIRQCmd, allowing the
interrupt chain to adopt it, then schedule camera alignment.
Align the camera axis perpendicular to travel: Y for horizontal doors, X for
vertical doors. Each unfinished call moves that coordinate by one pixel toward
a $100-pixel boundary; low bytes $80..$FF increment, $01..$7F decrement.
The unaligned word load places the coordinate's pixel low byte in A's high byte.
Immediate BIT #$FF00 tests it for zero but preserves the load's N flag for BMI.
Both paths refresh scrolling. A step reaching alignment still returns first;
only an already-aligned entry selects FixDoorsMovingUp.
Select the room-data bank and preserve elevator-related explored-map state
around loading the destination room and state headers. Initialise room effects
and decompress level/scroll/CRE data before scheduling scrolling setup.
This is one phase of state $0B, not the complete destination-room setup.
Wait for all music-queue timer words to clear; this is not a test that the
currently playing track has ended. Once clear, select the Samus-placement
correction phase and request the destination music only if the track changed.
Run destination-room animated tiles, enemies and enemy projectiles while
interpolating colors toward the room's target palette. Draw Samus through the
inanimate path rather than her ordinary state handlers. When the palette helper
returns carry set, restore sound queuing, clear transition flags and select
gameplay state $08. This is distinct from the pause/unpause brightness fades.
Read the fixed eleven-byte room header in bank $8F, then select a room state
from the condition-function stream that follows it. Width and height are stored
in screen units and multiplied by sixteen for block dimensions. The hardware
multiplier uses only each block dimension's low byte; double its word result
to obtain LevelDataSize in bytes. This routine does not decompress level data.
Load the selected state's resource pointers, music, FX, enemy population/set,
layer-2 scroll-control bytes and cached room-main callback. Long pointers are
assembled with overlapping word stores: high word first, then the low word.
The population chooses placements/parameters; the enemy set chooses graphics
and palettes. PLMs, library backgrounds and setup ASM are read by later loaders.
Walk bank-$8F condition functions starting eleven bytes after the room header.
Each function word is followed by that condition's own payload; X points at
the payload when the function runs. PEA supplies an RTS return to the loop.
A failed condition advances X past its payload and returns with RTS. A match
jumps to Use_StatePointer_inX, which drops that near return and exits with RTL.
X is the chosen state-header address, not the address of a pointer to dereference.
The default condition reaches this routine with X immediately after its own
function word, at the inline default state header. Matching non-default checks
instead load X from their payload's state pointer. Discard the scan loop's
two-byte return before RTL returns to the selector's long caller.
This condition's payload is one event byte followed by a two-byte state pointer.
On success select that pointed-to state through the common long-return exit.
On failure skip all three payload bytes and RTS back to the condition scan.
Read the optional PLM list from state offset $14. Six-byte records contain a
PLM ID, X/Y block bytes and argument word; a zero ID terminates the list.
Attempt each spawn without checking its carry result, then execute door ASM
and room setup ASM in that order, even when the PLM list was absent or empty.
Finally set ElevatorStatus to 2 only when the door's elevator property is set.
State offset $18 is an optional bank-$8F setup callback. A zero word skips it;
otherwise JSR invokes the setup routine, which returns with RTS. Restore the
saved data bank and processor status before RTL returns to the long caller.
This wrapper expects the state-header data to be readable in the entry data bank.
Read the optional door-ASM word from bank-$83 door data, but execute it in
bank $8F. For a nonzero pointer, PEA builds the callback's near RTS return
before the indirect JMP. The wrapper then restores bank/status and returns
with RTL. This is distinct from the room-state setup and main callbacks.
Execute the cached bank-$8F room-main word pointer when it is nonzero.
Set X to zero for the indexed indirect JSR, and restore the caller's data bank
after the callback's RTS. Unlike setup/door wrappers, this entry has no PHP/PLP
or register-width setup; it relies on the calling gameplay path's register mode.
Prepare enemy graphics/palettes and clear the base runtime enemy records before
Initialise_Enemies fills population slots and calls Init AI. The enemy set and
population are separate resources. Reset room-level enemy hooks and bookkeeping,
process the set and load tile data into RAM, then clear inherited sprite objects.
Door transitions have already loaded enemy VRAM graphics on an earlier path.
Zero $0800 bytes of base enemy records: each word write advances X twice and
decrements the byte counter twice. Then inspect the first population ID.
An immediate $FFFF skips enemy-set processing; a nonempty population processes
the graphics/palette set before returning. This does not call enemy Init AI.
Enter with word-sized registers. First clear $1400 words ($2800 bytes) from
EnemyTileData at $7E:7000 through $7E:97FF, then reset projectile bookkeeping.
For each $10-byte population record, fill a $40-byte runtime slot from header
defaults and placement fields, expose the slot in EnemyIndex and call Init AI.
The generic init word at population offset $06 first occupies Enemy.instList;
some Init AI, including Zoomer, reads it as flags rather than an address.
The AI can change these fields. After it returns, reset/select the placeholder
spritemap, advance both cursors and stop at $FFFF. Only the nonempty-list tail
records FirstFreeEnemyIndex, the listed count and the terminator's kill byte.
The earlier JSL supplied the long return frame for Init AI's RTL. Select the
AI data bank with the swapped-word push and two bank pulls, then tail-jump
through EnemyAIPointer. The caller restores its saved bank and X/Y cursors.
Match the population's enemy ID against four-byte enemy-set entries. Prior
entries contribute tile counts from their header size divided by $20. A match
supplies the palette index and accumulated graphics offset for the runtime
slot and its spawn-data mirror. A missing match uses offset zero and $0A00
palette attributes. Population position/parameters are not graphics metadata.
Prepare destination graphics and objects, executing PLMs/door/setup ASM before
loading and initialising enemies. The room-main callback is not invoked here.
This phase can wait inside one call: IRQ handles the pending FX transfer and
door scrolling, and their flags release the two busy loops. After scrolling,
run PLMs and explicitly wait for NMI before selecting the next transition phase.
PLMs run after the final scroll update; see the visibility caveat below.
Do not return to state $0B while waiting here. IRQ scrolling continues to run
and sets bit 15 on completion. Only then restore scrolling HDMA, process PLMs
and wait for NMI. These IRQ-driven waits are not the WaitForNMI request handshake.
Build separate active and interaction lists of runtime slot offsets, each ending
in $FFFF. Scan 32 base records at $40-byte intervals, skipping empty/respawn
slots and clearing deletion-marked IDs. Ordinary processing allows property
$0800 or frozen-AI bit $0004 to bypass viewport culling; property $0400 omits
the slot from the logical interaction list without omitting its AI.
The global offscreen override takes a different scan with no viewport tests.
The override still skips empty/respawn/deleted slots. It also writes each active
slot into InteractiveEnemyIndices at the active-list offset before testing
$0400. The separate interaction cursor controls accepted logical insertions and
the final sentinel; retain the distinction between this extra store and that
logical list. This path is not the ordinary visibility path with one flag changed.
Consume the active list selected earlier, performing collision checks, AI,
script updates and drawing-queue eligibility as separate stages. Do not equate
an active slot with an interactive or drawable one. The early zero-population
path still reaches sprite-object handling and collision-bookkeeping cleanup.
Global frozen time and the per-enemy frozen-AI flag are different conditions.
Only branches arriving here apply this pre-AI paralysis skip. Intangible slots,
nonzero invincibility timers and the debug interaction bypass instead enter
.interactEnd directly. The later .processAIEnd paralysis/death test is separate.
Enemy.AI = 0 selects the main-AI word at header offset $18. Otherwise select
one plus the zero-based index of the lowest set bit, then read $18 + 2*index:
bit 0 selects grapple AI ($1A), bit 1 hurt AI ($1C), bit 2 frozen AI ($1E).
Higher bits continue the same arithmetic without a validity mask. The earlier
global frozen-time path bypasses this selector and uses header offset $20.
The caller's JSL supplied the long return frame. Refresh the pointer's bank,
select the enemy's data bank and tail-jump through EnemyAIPointer. Its RTL
returns after that JSL; the caller restores the header bank and skips over
this inline helper before rechecking frozen time and processing instructions.
Extended spritemaps bypass the ordinary visibility helper. Other slots must
pass its radius-padded X and fixed-margin Y tests. Then property bits $0100/
$0200 and drawing-disable bit 0 can still prevent queue insertion.
The layer queue contains slot-offset words for a later drawing pass, not OAM.
Advance the selected enemy's script only when AI bit $0004 is clear and the
pre-decremented instruction timer becomes zero. A negative script word is a
bank-local command; a nonnegative word begins a four-byte duration/spritemap
record. The caller supplies EnemyAIPointer's bank byte; this routine sets its
command word and the script data bank. Enter with the expected word register mode.
PHK/PEA create a long return to the fetch loop. Commands normally RTL there,
but terminating commands replace the return word to reach the shared exit.
A timer initially zero wraps to $FFFF on decrement; it is not an immediate tick.
Accept the fetched word as duration, install the following spritemap word and
advance the saved cursor by four bytes. Set properties2 bit $8000 on this path;
the nonzero-timer path clears it. Frozen-AI and terminating-command exits do
not perform that same marker update.
Return A=0/Z set when these viewport tests pass, A=1/Z clear otherwise.
Horizontal bounds include XHitboxRadius; vertical bounds use Y+8 and camera
Y+$F8, not YHitboxRadius. These match the ordinary activity scan's tests.
Comparisons branch on the subtraction result's N flag as written; this is
not a general-purpose signed-coordinate rectangle test.
Append the current runtime slot offset to the queue selected by Enemy.layer.
The layer indexes an eight-word base-address table; queue sizes are byte counts
and increase by two per appended word. This routine does not draw the sprite
or append a sentinel, and has no layer/capacity bounds check.
Y points to the destination parameter word after the fetched command. Replace
Y with that word and RTL to the interpreter loop, which fetches at the new cursor.
Y points to the destination parameter word after the fetched command. Replace
Y with that word and RTL to the interpreter loop, which fetches at the new cursor.
Set Enemy.loopCounter from the parameter word and advance Y by two.
This loop counter is separate from Enemy.instTimer's graphical/wait duration.
Set Enemy.loopCounter from the parameter word and advance Y by two.
This loop counter is separate from Enemy.instTimer's graphical/wait duration.
Pre-decrement the loop-counter word. A nonzero result reuses the goto command
with the current target parameter; zero skips that parameter and continues.
Neither path ends this interpreter call or changes the spritemap directly.
Pre-decrement the loop-counter word. A nonzero result reuses the goto command
with the current target parameter; zero skips that parameter and continues.
Neither path ends this interpreter call or changes the spritemap directly.
Y starts after this command word. Rewind it by two and save the sleep command's
address in Enemy.instList. Replace the interpreter loop's return word with its
shared exit word, keeping the synthetic bank byte, then RTL out of this call.
This command does not set Enemy.instTimer or change the spritemap.
Y starts after this command word. Rewind it by two and save the sleep command's
address in Enemy.instList. Replace the interpreter loop's return word with its
shared exit word, keeping the synthetic bank byte, then RTL out of this call.
This command does not set Enemy.instTimer or change the spritemap.
Load Enemy.instTimer from the duration parameter, save the cursor after it and
terminate this interpreter call by replacing the synthetic return word.
The current spritemap is retained. This differs from a graphical record,
which installs a new spritemap and performs the graphical-update marker write.
Load Enemy.instTimer from the duration parameter, save the cursor after it and
terminate this interpreter call by replacing the synthetic return word.
The current spritemap is retained. This differs from a graphical record,
which installs a new spritemap and performs the graphical-update marker write.
Set property $0200 and exit this interpreter call through a replaced return word.
The command does not clear Enemy.ID itself. Activity selection later removes
deletion-marked slots; drawing eligibility also rejects that property bit.
Set property $0200 and exit this interpreter call through a replaced return word.
The command does not clear Enemy.ID itself. Activity selection later removes
deletion-marked slots; drawing eligibility also rejects that property bit.
PLM_BlockIndices stores a byte offset into the room's word-sized level data.
Halve it to a linear block number, then divide by the room width using the
SNES hardware divider. The quotient is the zero-based Y block and the
remainder is X. Six NOPs provide the divider's required result latency.
Scan the forty even PLM slots from $4E down to zero and fail with carry set
when none is free. A room population row supplies ID, byte X/Y and a word
argument. Convert Y * room-width + X to the level-data byte offset.
The ID addresses a bank-$84 PLM header: its first word is setup code and its
second word is the initial instruction list. Initialise the slot before calling
setup with X = header address and Y = slot; a successful spawn returns carry clear.
Run only while PLM_Flag has bit 15 set. Reset the shared draw-tilemap cursor
once per handler call, then visit occupied PLM slots from $4E down to zero.
PLM_Index is the durable current-slot identity because setup, pre-instructions
and instruction handlers freely reuse X. Empty slots are skipped.
Call the slot's pre-instruction on every eligible handler pass, then reload X
from PLM_Index. Pre-decrement the 16-bit instruction timer; only zero advances
the list. Starting from zero therefore wraps to $FFFF rather than advancing.
A list word with bit 15 set is bank-$84 code. PEA installs a synthetic near
return to the fetch loop and indirect JMP dispatches it; an ordinary RTS resumes.
A nonnegative list word is a frame duration followed by a draw-instruction
pointer. Save both, advance the list cursor four bytes and immediately apply
the draw instruction to level data. Then derive block coordinates and enqueue
the PLM's visible tilemap. Duration zero is not an immediate next-frame record:
the following pre-decrement wraps it to $FFFF.
Y begins after the command word. Rewind and save the sleep command as the
slot's instruction cursor. PLA discards the synthetic fetch-loop return, so
the final RTS exits Process_PLM through its original caller return.
The expired zero timer wraps to $FFFF on later passes until something wakes
the PLM by replacing its cursor or timer.
Clear the slot's ID so the outer handler treats it as free. As with sleep,
discard the synthetic fetch-loop return and RTS directly out of Process_PLM.
The parallel slot arrays need not be cleared because the zero ID owns liveness.
Treat the room argument as a global item-bit index. A negative argument
deliberately behaves as not collected. Otherwise convert the bit index to an
SRAM byte and mask, restoring the PLM slot X before testing the result.
A set bit follows the instruction-list target; an unset bit skips that word.
For a nonnegative room argument, set its global collected-item bit in the SRAM
mirror without disturbing neighbouring flags. Negative arguments suppress the
write. Item scripts perform this before granting the pickup and message.
A visible missile tank first branches to the empty-item path when its room-argument
bit was already collected. Otherwise it installs the pickup continuation as its
link target and a trigger-wait pre-instruction. The triggered continuation sets
the collected bit before clearing queued music and awarding five missiles.
A PLM draw instruction is a sequence of counted block runs applied directly
to LevelData. Bit 15 of a run header selects a column; clear selects a row.
The low byte is the block count and the following words are complete level
block values. Rows advance one word; columns advance one room-width row.
A zero word terminates the drawing. Otherwise the next two bytes are signed
X and Y block offsets from the PLM's original block. Sign-extend X and scale
it by two bytes per level word; multiply signed Y by room width and then by
two. The following run header begins immediately after that offset pair.
Use the native BG1 tilemap bases $5000 and $53E0 for PLM rendering, then
enter the shared renderer with Y at the current draw instruction. The second
base is intentionally $20 below $5400; later screen-half arithmetic accounts
for the split without masking the horizontal block coordinate again.
Start every draw-entry position from the PLM's block coordinates. Convert the
Layer 1 camera Y position to blocks and reject entries below its 16-row window.
Horizontal and vertical runs then clip their other axis before reserving VRAM
write-table space. Offscreen level-data changes therefore need no tilemap upload.
Clear the orientation bit to obtain the horizontal block count. Clip the run
against the camera's current 17-column update span, retaining a left-skip count
for its draw-data cursor. A run contained in one BG1 screen uses two VRAM writes
for its top and bottom tile rows; a screen-boundary crossing can require four.
Each level word uses its low ten bits as a metatile index. Multiply by eight
to select four word-sized entries in TileTable. Bits $0400 and $0800 request
horizontal and vertical flips: reorder the 2x2 quadrants and toggle tilemap
flip bits $4000/$8000. Each expanded block consumes eight staging bytes.
Clear the orientation bit for the vertical block count and require the column
to lie inside the camera's horizontal update span. Clip blocks above and below
the visible rows, then use two column-mode VRAM writes for the left and right
tile columns. Metatile flip handling mirrors the horizontal path's semantics.
After a visible run, restore the caller's X and advance past the run's source
words. A zero offset pair ends the draw instruction. Otherwise sign-extend the
next X/Y bytes relative to the original PLM block and render that entry with
the same clipping and upload rules.
Map a visible block row and wrapped 32-column block coordinate into the BG1
tilemap destination. Each block contributes two tile rows and two tile columns.
BG1XOffset bit 8 selects which $400-word screen half is currently displayed;
crossing column $10 and that scroll bit choose the opposite half consistently.
Build two VRAM write records for a run contained in one screen half. Horizontal
mode targets two tile rows; vertical mode ORs $8000 for column increment and
targets adjacent columns. Each record copies four bytes per metatile from the
bank-$7E PLMDrawTilemap staging buffer at its current shared write index.
Consume the seven-byte VRAMWrite records prepared by main-thread systems.
VRAMWriteStack is the byte offset after the last record; write a zero-size
terminator there, then walk records from offset zero. Each record supplies a
word size, 24-bit source and VRAM destination to DMA channel 1 in mode 1.
The destination word's sign bit selects the VRAM increment mode. A clear bit
uses $80, advancing one word after the high-byte write; a set bit uses $81,
advancing 32 words for column uploads. Write the same destination to VMADD,
trigger channel 1, then advance seven bytes to the next software record.
Reset the ordinary write-table stack after consuming it. Horizontal and
vertical scrolling buffers are independent flag-driven queues, so process
both even when VRAMWriteStack was already zero. The caller's processor
status is restored after all three upload paths finish.
Upload newly exposed BG1 columns with VMAIN $81: DMA writes each word's low
and high bytes, then advances 32 VRAM words to the next tilemap row. Separate
left/right staging buffers target adjacent columns. Upload the unwrapped
segment first, followed by the optional segment that wrapped in tilemap VRAM.
BG2 repeats the BG1 column geometry with its own flag, sizes, destinations and
bank-$7E staging buffers. Clear the flag before DMA so this prepared update is
consumed once. A zero wrapped size skips only the wrapped pair; the unwrapped
left/right transfers have already completed.
Upload newly exposed BG1 rows with VMAIN $80, advancing one VRAM word after
each tilemap word. The top-half buffer uses the prepared destination; OR $20
selects the next 32-word tile row for the bottom-half buffer. Repeat that pair
from adjusted sources and a second destination when the row wraps in VRAM.
BG2 has the same top/bottom and unwrapped/wrapped row layout as BG1, using its
own prepared buffers. Every transfer uses WRAM bank $7E and DMA channel 1.
Clear the update flag once, then a zero wrapped size bypasses the wrapped pair
without affecting the unwrapped upload already sent.
The preceding SEP #$02 sets the processor's zero flag, so BEQ always skips
this self-loop on a conforming 65816. Preserve the loop as an unreachable
status-flag sentinel from the original program; it is not a data-dependent
failure check in the normal BG2 wrapped-row transfer.
Consume nine-byte VRAMRead records during the serviced NMI path. A record
provides the VRAM word address, DMA mode and B-bus target, 24-bit WRAM
destination and byte count. Channel 1 performs the VRAM-to-WRAM transfer,
then the reader advances by the exact nine-byte software-record stride.
VRAMReadStack is the byte offset after the final record. With the accumulator
still eight-bit, STZ writes only one zero byte at that offset, but the loop
later tests a word source after REP #$20. This retained mismatch is safe only
when the following byte is already zero; normal producers queue one read.
Scan all eight word-sized timer slots from offset $0E down to zero. Carry is
set when any slot has a nonzero timer and clear only when every timer is zero.
This reports queued countdowns; it does not inspect the active music timer,
the ring indices or whether the SPC is currently playing a track.
Advance the active music countdown and the eight-slot word-indexed ring.
A positive timer keeps waiting, zero dispatches the active entry, and a
negative timer loads the next queued entry. When the ring is empty, store
zero so the next call underflows and checks the queue again.
A nonnegative entry is an SPC track request. Send its low seven bits through
$2140, mirror the track number and suppress sound-effect handshakes for eight
calls. Clear the consumed ring slot, advance its byte offset by two modulo
$10, then immediately load the next queued entry if one exists.
A negative entry selects a music-data upload by its low byte. Build the
24-bit source from overlapping words in Music_Pointers and synchronously
upload it to the SPC. Mark $FF while uploading, then clear the marker, consume
the ring slot and impose eight calls of sound-effect downtime before returning.
Service the three independent sound-library handshakes after game-state logic.
Each library owns one SPC port ($2141..$2143), a 16-byte ring and a state byte.
When music has imposed downtime, decrement that counter and keep all three
request ports and current-sound mirrors clear instead of advancing states.
The per-library state byte indexes this word-pointer table. States send a
queued request, wait for the SPC to echo it, delay before clearing the port,
wait for the echoed clear, or perform the separate delayed reset path. The
selected bank-$82 handler returns with RTS to the three-library dispatch loop.
For library index 0, 1 or 2, compare its ring start and next indices. The
$00/$10/$20 table selects that library's 16-byte queue while X selects its
adjacent metadata and SPC port. Send one sound, advance the start modulo $10
and enter acknowledgement state 1; an empty queue remains in state 0.
Wait until the selected SPC port echoes the current sound ID. Reassert the
request while it differs. On acknowledgement, enter state 2 and install a
two-call clear delay; the queue entry was already consumed when it was sent.
Count down the selected library's two-call hold after request acknowledgement.
When it expires, clear both the SPC request port and its current-sound mirror,
then enter state 3 to wait for the SPC to echo that clear.
Wait until the selected SPC port matches the now-zero current-sound mirror,
rewriting zero while it does not. Once acknowledged, reset to state 0 and
tail-branch into the sender so another queued sound can begin in this call.
If state 4 is selected, it uses the same per-library clear counter as state 2.
It returns to state 0 only when that counter reaches zero; unlike the normal
state-2 path, it does not write the SPC port or current-sound mirror here.
Clear the three adjacent start bytes, next bytes and state bytes with four
overlapping word stores plus the final state-3 byte store. Queue payloads and
SPC ports are not erased here; equal zero indices make every ring logically
empty, and state 0 leaves each library idle until a new request is queued.
Queue a word-sized track or music-data request with an eight-call delay.
Reject demo game states ($28 and above), and reserve one of the eight ring
slots so the wrapped next index can never equal the consumer index. A full
ring drops this request without changing entries or either cursor.
Queue the request at the current producer offset with max(Y, 8) calls of
delay. Demo states are still rejected, but this variant does not compare the
next and start indices before writing. It can overwrite an unread slot and
always advances the producer by one word modulo the eight-slot ring.
Store either Y or the clamped minimum of eight in the timer slot paired with
the request. Advance the word offset by two and mask with $000E, producing
the ring sequence $00, $02, ... $0E, $00 without a capacity check.
The library-1 wrappers preserve X, Y and status, switch to byte registers and
move the caller's sound ID into A high. Loading 15, 9, 6, 3 or 1 into A low
selects the maximum outstanding count before branching into the common body.
The common return restores the stack frame created by whichever wrapper ran.
Queue one library-1 sound when its modulo-16 outstanding count is below the
wrapper's threshold. XBA recovers the sound ID after the count check. Global
sound disable, demo states and an active power-bomb explosion each reject the
request before any ring byte or producer index changes.
Y is the current producer slot and X is its wrapped successor. When advancing
would not collide with the consumer, store the sound at Y, publish X as the
new producer and clear that next slot as the queue sentinel.
The retained physical-full path calls an empty hook, then compares the new
sound ID with the byte at the current producer slot. Only a numerically lower
ID replaces that byte, and the producer index remains unchanged. Official
threshold wrappers normally reject a consistent full ring before this path.
Library-2 wrappers use the same packed A convention and thresholds as library
1: the sound ID moves into A high and the maximum outstanding count occupies
A low. The common library-2 body restores X, Y and status on every exit.
Apply the threshold and global sound gates to library 2's independent start,
next and 16-byte ring. The arithmetic and control flow mirror library 1, but
all capacity state and payload bytes belong exclusively to library 2.
Commit a library-2 request only when the wrapped successor does not equal its
consumer index. The published next slot is cleared after insertion, retaining
the zero sentinel expected by subsequent producers.
The library-2 full-ring branch shares the empty hook and numeric comparison.
A lower ID may replace the current producer byte without advancing the ring;
an equal or higher ID is discarded through the common restoring return.
Library-3 wrappers repeat the packed sound/threshold ABI and shared restore
frame. Their only data difference is the independent library-3 metadata and
payload ring selected by the common body below.
Apply the same modulo-16 threshold, global-disable, demo and power-bomb gates
to library 3. Successful requests modify only its producer index and 16-byte
queue; the consumer later sends them through SPC port $2143.
Store the library-3 sound at its current producer slot, advance modulo 16 and
clear the new producer slot when that advance does not collide with the start.
On the retained library-3 collision path, keep the producer fixed and replace
its current byte only when the new sound ID is numerically lower. All exits
restore the wrapper's processor status, Y and X in that order.
Decode the eight data bytes placed immediately after the caller's JSL:
channel, DMA mode, B-bus target, 24-bit source and 16-bit byte count.
The helper selects that channel's $43x0 register block, writes the descriptor
without starting DMA, then advances the stacked return address past the data.
Map channel numbers 0..7 to the corresponding $4300..$4370 register-block
offset. Callers still start the configured transfer through $420B or $420C.
Publish the prepared CPU/PPU shadow bytes during the serviced NMI. Ordinary
registers are copied once; scroll and Mode 7 words are sent low byte then high
byte through the hardware write latches. Gameplay screen and colour-math copies
retain the values actually presented by this frame.
Upload the four Mode 7 matrix coefficients and two origins only when either the
real or fake BG-mode shadow selects mode 7. Each word uses the PPU register's
two-write latch, preserving the matrix/origin state prepared outside NMI.
Configure channel 0 to copy all $220 bytes of the software OAM image to $2104
and channel 1 to copy the full $200-byte palette image to $2122. Reset both
hardware destinations to zero, then start the two independent DMAs together.
Consume pending top- and bottom-half Samus tile definitions with DMA channel 1.
Each seven-byte definition supplies a 24-bit source followed by two byte counts;
the second part is optional and begins immediately after the first source range.
Top data targets VRAM $6000/$6100 and bottom data targets $6080/$6180.
Independently test the bottom-half request and repeat the same one- or two-part
descriptor transfer at the bottom-half VRAM destinations. A zero second size
skips only the optional second DMA.
When animated-tile objects are enabled, scan their six word-indexed slots from
$0A down to zero. A live object with a pending source address uploads its bank-$87
graphics through DMA channel 0 to the prepared VRAM word address.
Skip empty objects and slots with no newly prepared graphics. After a transfer,
clear only the source address so the request is consumed once while the animated
tile object itself remains active.
Any release or change in the complete input word reloads the initial repeat delay.
After that delay expires, the unchanged input word is copied to fake-new and the
shorter subsequent delay is reloaded. Real new-input remains edge-only.
The retained conditional debug path repeats the same edge/repeat bookkeeping for
controller 2, handles the four-button soft-reset chord when audio is not uploading,
and then interprets controller-1 debug chords without changing the ordinary sampler.
A new Start or A press restores the seven configurable gameplay bindings to the
vanilla X/A/B/Y/Select/R/L masks, then rebuilds and redraws the menu's temporary
binding-index array.
Convert each live gameplay button mask to the menu's compact index representation:
X=0, A=1, B=2, Select=3, Y=4, L=5 and R=6. The seven entries remain ordered by
action: shot, jump, dash, item select, item cancel, aim up and aim down.
This table is the shared action order used while loading and saving the controller
settings menu. Item Select precedes Item Cancel even though their default masks are
Select and Y respectively.
Convert all seven temporary menu indices back to SNES button masks and write them
through the parallel action-address table. This is the point where an options-menu
swap becomes the live gameplay binding state.
Map compact menu indices to hardware joypad bits. The first seven entries are valid
configurable action buttons; Left and Right follow for other menu input uses.
Scan newly pressed configurable buttons from R back through X, convert the selected
table offset to its compact index and search the six other actions for its owner.
Bindings form a seven-button permutation, so the selected button already belongs to
exactly one row. Exchange that row's index with the current action instead of creating
a duplicate; this is why assigning Select to Item Cancel moves Y to Item Select.
Normalize the requested slot to 0..2, refresh the WRAM save mirror with live
equipment/options, explored maps, load station and area, then copy its complete
word range to that slot's SRAM offset. Sum every word modulo $10000 while copying.
Before compacting map data, copy the current area's $100-byte working map into
its area slice in the full explored-map array. SaveMap then exports only the
listed meaningful bytes for all areas into the SRAM mirror.
Copy every mirror word into the chosen slot and accumulate its 16-bit checksum.
Store two identical checksum copies and two identical one's-complement copies;
the loader accepts either checksum/complement pair.
Copy the selected SRAM slot into the WRAM mirror while recomputing the word sum.
Validate the primary checksum and complement first, then fall back to the second
pair. A valid slot is committed to live state only after one pair passes.
For a valid slot, copy the $60-byte equipment/options region into live low RAM,
expand the saved map representation, restore station and area, and return carry
clear. Validation never partially publishes a corrupt mirror.
If both checksum pairs fail, overwrite the complete selected SRAM slot with zero,
reset station and area to zero, and return carry set. Live equipment and map data
are intentionally not copied from the invalid mirror.
The three slots begin at SRAM offsets $0010, $066C and $0CC8. The caller's slot
number is doubled before indexing this word table.
Add the requested energy to the main tank. Overflow beyond MaxEnergy is redirected
into reserve energy up to MaxReserveEnergy; any nonzero reserve fill also changes
an off reserve-tank mode to auto before clamping the main tank.
Apply raw damage without suit reduction. Negative input enters the crash handler,
$012C is a retained no-damage sentinel, frozen time suppresses subtraction, and
a result below zero is clamped to exactly zero.
Consume the pending signed 16.16 periodic-damage amount used by heat, liquids,
spikes and several enemy contacts. Varia divides it by two and Gravity by four;
the subtraction borrows from fractional SubUnitEnergy into whole Energy.
Pending periodic damage is one-shot. Clear both fractional and whole words after
application, when time is frozen, or after lethal underflow has clamped health.
Treat energy below 31 as critical. Crossing down queues sound 2 and sets the warning
flag; crossing back up clears it and queues sound 1. Queue rejection can leave the
flag and actual SPC sound out of sync, matching the retained game behavior.
Count consecutive held-jump samples, snapshot held/new input for drawing logic and
compare Energy with its previous sample. A decrease starts hurt flashing when no
flash is active; the conditional debug-invincibility path may restore old energy.
At zero or negative energy, automatic reserve mode with reserve energy freezes time
and enters game state $1B. Otherwise normal gameplay locks Samus for death and enters
state $13. Non-gameplay states return instead of repeatedly starting death.
Independently tick in-game time using the regional FPS constant, cascading through
seconds and minutes at 60 and hours thereafter. Values at or above 100 hours clamp
to 99:59:59 plus the final frame value 59.
Transfer one reserve-energy unit to the main tank per call, queueing the refill sound
every eight serviced NMI frames. Stop and zero reserve when the main tank reaches its
maximum or reserve is exhausted; carry reports completion.
Clear all ten word-indexed projectile/bomb slots, install the inert pre-instruction
and reset global projectile, bomb, cooldown and power-bomb state. Door transitions
and elevators use this to discard the prior room's active projectile runtime.
Zero one slot's complete position, velocity, collision, type, damage, instruction and
drawing state, then install the inert pre-instruction. Slots below $0A decrement the
projectile counter; slots $0A and above decrement the bomb counter, both saturating.
Turn beams and missiles into explosion objects while clearing other projectile types.
A beam first moves its origin to the directional collision edge using its radii;
missiles already use their current origin. Both then receive inert movement.
Visit all ten slots from word offset $12 down to zero. A nonzero instruction pointer
marks an active slot: run its bank-$90 pre-instruction, then its bank-$93 instruction
handler, reloading the shared index after code that may repurpose X.
Resolve a beam, missile, hyper beam or ice-SBA type into its projectile-data record.
Beam low-nibble combinations select charged or uncharged tables; non-beams select by
the type high nibble. Direction chooses one of the record's instruction-list pointers.
Load damage from the record, reject a negative sentinel, then select the direction's
instruction list. Its first frame supplies byte-sized X/Y radii at offsets 4 and 5;
an instruction timer of one schedules immediate interpretation.
Select bomb or power-bomb projectile data from the non-beam type nibble, load damage
and the record's single instruction-list pointer, and schedule its first command.
Convert a killed beam to category $07 or a missile/super missile to category $08,
select the matching explosion instruction list and sound, and give the explosion
damage 8. Super missiles additionally start earthquake type $14 for 30 ticks.
If the global shot cooldown is 21 or greater, lower it to 20 so the explosion path
does not retain a longer delay. Shorter existing cooldowns remain unchanged.
Add the requested missiles to the live count. Values beyond normal capacity spill
into the otherwise rarely used reserve-missile word before the live count clamps
to maximum. An under-capacity result leaves reserve missiles untouched.
Reserve missiles cap at the lesser of 99 and maximum missile capacity. Maximums
below 99 use the equipment capacity; maximums of 99 or more use the hard 99 cap.
Add the requested super missiles and clamp only values strictly above maximum.
Equality returns directly because the provisional live count is already correct.
Add the requested power bombs and clamp only values strictly above maximum, using
the same equality-preserving structure as super-missile restoration.
Tick a positive global projectile cooldown toward zero and canonicalize negative
values to zero. While time is frozen, replace it with 32 every call so firing
cannot become immediately available when the normal tick path is suspended.
Allow a beam only below the five-projectile limit and when the cooldown low byte
is zero. Success reserves ownership immediately by setting cooldown to one and
incrementing the projectile counter; carry reports whether the caller may continue.
Normal missiles share the five-projectile limit with beams. Super missiles require
the count to be below four because firing also creates a linked projectile slot.
Both use the same cooldown test and reserve one counter unit before returning success.
The firing gates inspect only the cooldown's low byte. Higher-byte state is retained
by this historical contract and does not by itself block a reservation.
Tick the active slot's instruction timer. On expiry, interpret negative words as
bank-$93 commands and nonnegative words as eight-byte timed frame records containing
duration, spritemap, byte-sized X/Y radii and the next instruction cursor.
Commands receive Y pointing after their opcode. A synthetic near return sends RTS
back to the interpreter loop, allowing commands to change Y or consume arguments.
A delete command instead removes that return and exits the long handler directly.
Clear the current projectile, discard the interpreter's synthetic near return, then
restore the handler's saved bank/status and return directly to its long caller.
Replace Y with the word pointer stored at the command argument and return to the
interpreter loop. The target is a bank-$93 instruction-list address.
Visit the five ordinary projectile slots from word offset 8 down to zero. Inactive
slots and bomb/explosion categories are skipped. Beam combinations without a charge
or non-beam category alternate frames by slot parity to reduce sprite pressure.
Visit all ten slots but draw only categories $03 and above: bombs, power bombs and
projectile explosions. Power bombs with a zero bomb timer remain hidden. Ordinary
coordinates use a wider horizontal cull before OAM submission.
Ceres rotation paths calculate screen position through the rotating-room helper.
Normal paths subtract layer-1 scroll. A negative spritemap pointer is submitted only
when the computed Y coordinate is on the visible byte page; offscreen paths retain
the original no-op long call.
Redirect permanent Hyper Beam mode to its separate firing path. Otherwise reserve a
beam slot and cooldown through the shared firing gate. A failed charged-enough attempt
stops the resume-charge sound and queues the cannot-fire sound.
Choose the first ordinary slot whose damage word is zero, scanning offsets $00..$08.
The earlier counter gate should guarantee capacity; the retained fallback selects the
last ordinary slot if counter ownership and damage occupancy disagree.
Resolve pose-dependent origin/direction, set the projectile-invincibility window and
trail timer, then combine equipped beam bits with the live-projectile flag. Beam type
selects its sound and bank-$93 damage/instruction record.
Charge Beam or a newly pressed shot uses the ordinary per-beam cooldown table. Without
Charge Beam, a held auto-fire continuation uses the separate auto-fire table. Both
tables are byte-indexed by the low six projectile-type bits.
Begin with zero velocity for an immediate spawn-point block collision. Non-wave beams
may become an explosion and return before motion is installed. Surviving beams select
a pre-instruction by beam combination and then receive directional velocity.
The twelve valid low-nibble beam combinations choose straight/no-wave motion, the
uncharged ice-wave handler, or the shared wave/plasma/spazer handler.
Reserve a normal projectile slot through the shared beam gate. A failed attempt with
at least 16 ticks of prior charge stops the resume-charge sound and queues cannot-fire
feedback; shorter failed attempts return silently.
Choose a zero-damage ordinary slot, resolve origin/direction, then retain only the
charge-equipment bit and low beam combination before adding the live and charged-shot
type flags. The combination selects charged sound and bank-$93 projectile data.
Charged shots deliberately use `ProjectileCooldowns_Uncharged`, indexed by the low
six type bits after construction. The table name is retained source vocabulary; this
routine's type still has the charged bit set.
Probe the spawn point before installing motion. Non-wave beams that immediately become
an explosion skip movement setup; surviving beams select a pre-instruction and receive
directional velocity. Every completed construction path starts a four-tick glow.
All charged wave combinations use the shared wave/plasma/spazer/charged-ice-wave
handler. Charged combinations without wave use the straight no-wave handler.
Fire on either the current new-shot edge or the drawing-time copy of the preceding
edge. The shared gate reserves cooldown/counter ownership before ammunition and actual
slot occupancy are checked.
Undo the shared firing gate's counter reservation when selected ammunition is zero or
the five damage words contain no free slot. A later pose-direction failure follows the
retained direct-return path instead; normal gameplay poses supply a direction.
Choose the first zero-damage ordinary slot, resolve pose-dependent origin/direction,
set the 20-tick interaction window, and consume one missile or super missile only after
origin creation succeeds.
Move HUD selection 1/2 into the projectile category byte, add the live flag, and choose
the corresponding non-beam sound unless a cinematic suppresses it. Then initialise
velocity, bank-$93 projectile data, and missile/super-missile motion behavior.
Select missile or super-missile pre-instruction from category bit $0200. The category
nibble then indexes the byte cooldown table. Auto-cancel clears selection immediately;
otherwise the last unit of the selected ammunition clears it.
Find a second zero-damage ordinary slot, mark it as a live super-missile link, and copy
the primary projectile's position and direction before loading link data and behavior.
The earlier super-missile firing limit is what normally guarantees this slot.
Pack the link slot offset into the primary projectile variable's low byte while retaining
its high byte, then increment the ordinary projectile counter for the second owned slot.
While the configured shot button is held, route HUD item 3 to power bombs and every
other selection to the normal-bomb path. Releasing shot cancels any nonzero charge/flare
state, restores the suit palette and queues the cancellation sound.
Ask the bomb/spread gate to reserve ownership. On success, scan the five bomb slots at
offsets $0A..$12 for a zero type word; the counter gate should make the retained final-slot
fallback unnecessary during consistent runtime state.
Create category-$05 bomb state at Samus's position with direction zero and the regional
fuse reload. Bank $93 supplies damage/script data; the bank-$90 pre-instruction handles
the fuse, and category 5 selects its byte cooldown.
Reject while the signed active-power-bomb flag is negative. Otherwise reserve a bomb

power bombs remain selected while ammunition remains and clear after the final unit.

restores the suit palette and queues the charge-release sound. No single slot is reserved.

the later-bomb limit/cooldown checks; subsequent reservations require fewer than five
active bombs and a zero cooldown low byte.

replaces that provisional cooldown after construction. Failure cancels nonzero charge
state, clears flare animation, restores the suit palette and returns carry clear.

by $1C bytes to the late-fuse animation segment. At zero, queue the bomb sound and replace
the slot with its bank-$93 bomb-explosion instruction list.

the global power-bomb explosion effect.

to the slot timer. The retained routine continues through its normal return this frame.

the effect clears that flag, release the projectile slot through the shared clear routine.
Use the current pose's eight-byte definition record unless a one-shot transition shot
direction is pending; that override is consumed immediately. Direction bytes with a zero
high nibble are normal shot directions.
Store direction in the selected slot, use its low nibble to index signed X/Y origin
offsets, and subtract the pose definition's Y offset. Most poses use the default tables;
running and the two moonwalk poses use their shared alternate tables.
Direction marker $10 asks the previous different pose for a usable direction. Any other
nonzero high-nibble marker, or another special marker from that fallback pose, rejects
firing, decrements the earlier projectile-counter reservation and returns carry set.
Use the ordinary beam firing gate, scan the five normal slots for zero damage, and
resolve pose-dependent origin/direction. A rejected origin already undoes the gate's
counter reservation through the shared position routine.
Assign fixed type $9018, queue the charged sound selected by its plasma low nibble, and
load the matching charged bank-$93 record. Probe initial wave collision before forcing
damage to 1000 and installing Hyper Beam behavior and velocity.
A successful shot sets cooldown 21, a charged-glow word of $8014, and flare animation
frames/timers for the Hyper Beam presentation. Flare counter $8000 selects its separate
animation path.

separate countdown animation. On the first ordinary charge tick, initialize the main
flare and two spark components.
After 15 charge ticks, animate component 0; at tick 16 queue the charging sound. Delay
tables use byte $FF to restart at frame zero and $FE followed by a byte to move the frame
cursor backward. At 30 ticks, also animate components 2 and 4.

nonzero frames reload three ticks. Component 4 reaching frame zero clears the global flare
counter while all components are still offered to the shared drawing helper.

flare spritemap. The current pose supplies vertical offset and shot direction; marker $FF
or $10 suppresses drawing.
Direction selects signed flare origin offsets. Running uses alternate tables; other
movement uses defaults. Convert world position to layer-1 screen coordinates and subtract
the pose Y offset before submitting a visible byte-page Y coordinate.
In the rotating Ceres room, temporarily transform Samus's position through the shared
rotation helper, calculate/draw the flare from that transformed position, then restore
the original world coordinates.

palette are managed by the caller because cancellation, firing and Hyper Beam use
different presentation transitions.
Resolve the missile type's low-nibble data index, but deliberately seed base speed with
zero. Preserve the selected projectile slot in both scratch conventions before entering
the shared direction dispatcher. Missile acceleration supplies the launch speed later.
Clear both subpositions, reduce the direction to its low nibble, and dispatch through ten
word pointers. Directions 0/9 share up and 4/5 share down; the eight directional helpers
combine base speed with selected pieces of Samus's recent movement.

it becomes nonzero, add MissileInitializedBitset once per update and return. On the crossing
tick, initialize directional velocity; a super missile also creates its linked projectile.

super-missile table; otherwise use ordinary missile acceleration. Add both signed words to
the live velocities while preserving the caller's X and Y registers.
Upward shots negate base speed and optionally add a correction derived from the unaligned
word at ProjSpeed_SubDistanceSamusMovedRight+1. Its bytes span two movement fields; the
routine's shift/sign operations and retained low-byte contamination are documented as-is.
Right/down components add base speed to unaligned recent-movement words. These loads do not
represent clean 16-bit speeds: each starts at the second byte of one RAM field and consumes
the first byte of its neighbor. Preserve that original byte ordering when reviewing behavior.
Leftward shots negate base speed, then add CameraYSubSpeed+1. That unaligned word combines
the high byte of camera Y subspeed with the low byte of distance-moved-left; the apparently
unrelated low byte is real source behavior, not a normalized movement value.
Diagonal helpers calculate each axis independently using the same horizontal/vertical paths
as cardinal shots. Up-left combines the shifted upward correction with negated base speed
and the CameraYSubSpeed+1 leftward overlap; other diagonals use their corresponding pair.
Run link handling only for live super missiles ($0200) or their explosion category ($0800),
and only after the variable high byte marks initialization complete. The variable low byte
is the linked projectile slot offset used for the auxiliary collision probe.

ten, place the link behind the primary's current position, and move the link through the
ordinary missile collision helper. Slower live supers simply copy primary Y into the link.

absolute X velocity to decide whether an auxiliary probe is needed, then temporarily makes
the linked slot current while calling the horizontal missile mover.
Explosion category $0800 clears the linked projectile on both fast and slow paths instead
of synchronizing its coordinate. Live category $0200 keeps the link: fast paths retain the
collision-helper result, while slow paths copy the primary coordinate directly.
A nonzero direction high nibble is the shared deletion flag. Otherwise spawn a trail every
four updates, add the direction's X/Y acceleration pair, run the matching non-wave collision
wrapper, and finally cull the beam against the expanded viewport.

skips its vertical move when horizontal collision returns carry set, preventing a second
block interaction after the beam has already collided.
Ordinary missiles share the deletion flag, four-update trail cadence and direction-indexed
projectile acceleration used by beams. They then call the separate launch/acceleration state
machine, dispatch missile collision by direction, and finish with viewport culling.
Direction is doubled for the projectile-acceleration word tables, then halved back to its
numeric value across AccelerateMissile, and doubled again for collision-pointer dispatch.
The shared ProjectileIndex reloads the live slot after trail code may repurpose X.
Missile cardinal wrappers move one axis. Diagonals call horizontal movement first and call
vertical movement only when no horizontal collision occurred, mirroring the non-wave beam
ordering with missile-specific collision helpers.

state machine, and dispatches a collision wrapper by direction. A deletion flag or successful
offscreen cull enters group cleanup instead of leaving its linked slot behind.

$0200 entry. This removes both the primary and linked representation; it also means cleanup
is category-wide rather than limited to one stored link back-reference.

move vertically and update the vertical link path; if horizontal movement collided, still run
horizontal link cleanup/synchronization but skip the vertical axis.

clear the link, then perform the same five-slot category-$0200 sweep as primary cleanup so a
link-side collision cannot leave the primary active alone.

slots tick their respective fuse/effect handler, then run the shared bomb/explosion block
collision routine every update; fuse handling does not replace collision handling.

the common wave mover. Uncharged ice-wave uses a three-update trail cadence and deliberately
falls through to that same mover after reloading the slot.
Add the same direction-indexed X/Y acceleration pairs as non-wave beams, but dispatch to
wave-specific movement helpers that can pass through compatible blocks. Diagonal movement
still processes horizontal collision first and suppresses vertical movement on carry set.
Hyper Beam honors the same deletion flag, then jumps directly to common wave movement.
It does not pass through either periodic trail-entry routine; its separate firing/flare
presentation owns the visible effect state.

must each lie in [-64, 320); otherwise clear the slot and return carry set. A surviving
projectile returns carry clear so super-missile code can distinguish group cleanup.

diagonal speed, then the shared directional initializer combines that base with the retained
recent-movement words. The long-call wrapper establishes bank $90 and restores it on return.

$00..$1F, missile and super missile use $20/$21, and SBA trail variants use $24..$26.
Each entry independently selects one instruction list for each half of the trail pair.

are eligible; adding $1F maps missile/super categories 1/2 to table entries $20/$21. Other
categories return carry set without allocating a trail.

pair liveness. Initialize both timers to one, install left/right scripts, copy the projectile
origin through SetProjectileTrailPosition and return carry clear; exhaustion returns set.

addresses invoked with a synthetic return to the fetch loop; nonnegative words are durations
followed by tile/attribute data. A zero duration ends that half of the trail pair.

coordinates have high byte zero. A visible half appends one four-byte low-OAM entry; the
right half repeats the same interpreter and visibility checks independently.

checks, but never decrements timers, interprets commands or advances script cursors. Trail
animation and scripted position changes therefore pause while presentation remains visible.

either half's Y for downward drift or decrement the left half for upward drift, then RTS

whether to stop the charging sound. Hyper Beam or a loadout without Charge Beam simply

returns without creating a shot.

clears charge and component state and reloads the normal suit palette because the SBA now
owns projectile presentation.
